extracted.intended_audience: pipeline operators, pipeline industry stakeholders, regulatory compliance personnel, and legal/regulatory advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements from PHMSA's final rule regarding remotely or automatically controlled shut-off valves (RMVs), alternative equivalent technologies, valve spacing/locations, monitoring, maintenance, drills, and class‑location replacement applicability. Targets compliance actions for gas and hazardous liquid transmission pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve spacing for new gas pipeline construction
rubrics_metrics.description: For new gas pipeline construction, spacing of RMVs and alternative equivalent technology will follow existing requirements at §192.179(a) determining distance by reference to class location: 2.5-mile intervals in Class 4 locations, 4-mile intervals in Class 3 locations, 7.5-mile intervals in Class 2 locations, and 10-mile intervals in Class 1 locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA cites existing §192.179(a) as the standard for new construction. This is the baseline spacing; replacement-project allowances and other exceptions are discussed separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement-project valve spacing (‘one-class bump’ allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: For replacement projects on gas pipelines, operators are allowed to use the maximum valve spacing of a class below the class location of the replacement project. In practice: replacement projects in Class 4 locations can have spacing up to 8 miles; Class 3 up to 15 miles; and Class 1 and Class 2 up to 20 miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA extends the longstanding industry practice of a 'one-class bump' (per §192.611 procedures) to valve spacing for replacements to avoid forcing new spacing standards when operators are using pre-existing design standards. If spacing exceeds the next class location spacing, a new RMV/alternative equivalent technology is required. PHMSA will monitor data to ensure safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazardous liquid pipeline valve spacing (HVL)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA finalizes minimum valve spacing standards at every 15 miles for pipeline segments in, or which could affect, HCAs and at every 20 miles for pipeline segments that could not affect HCAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA based HVL spacing on ASME B31.4 recommendations and believes these standards are appropriate in populated areas. Operators may request exemptions or increases (see exemption/increase criteria). PHMSA allows a 25% increase in high-population/other populated areas upon PHMSA review and appropriate safety evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption/notification process for hazardous liquid spacing infeasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A hazardous liquid pipeline operator may request an exemption from spacing requirements by demonstrating that installing an RMV or alternative equivalent technology is economically, technically, or operationally infeasible, via notification procedures in §195.18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations may reference factors such as access to communications and power; terrain; prohibitive cost; component and labor availability; ability to secure access rights and necessary permits; and lack of accessibility to operator personnel. The notice must include a safety evaluation of deviation referencing technical/safety factors including design, construction, maintenance, operating procedures; potential consequences to environment/public; and mitigation measures (e.g., operating times for isolation valves). PHMSA may grant requests and requires record retention for the useful life of the pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance to increase HVL valve spacing by 25% in populated areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators may request (in accordance with §195.18 and subject to PHMSA review) an increase, by 25 percent, of the maximum valve spacing intervals for HVL pipeline segments in high-population areas or other populated areas where installation is not economically, technically, or operationally feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The operator must submit a safety evaluation referencing technical and safety factors (design, construction, maintenance, operations; potential consequences; mitigation measures). If granted, the operator must keep supporting records for the useful life of the pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve siting relative to flood plains and water crossings
rubrics_metrics.description: Valves must be installed outside of the 100-year flood plain of the body or bodies of water, or the valves must have actuators and other control equipment installed so as not to be impacted by flood conditions, or the equipment might be elevated to a level where they will not be impacted by flood conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA defines 'flood conditions' to include water level high enough to prevent actuation or damage electronics and debris carried by floodwaters. For multiple water crossings, operators must locate valves upstream and downstream of the first and last of multiple water crossings so that the total distance between the upstream-most valve and the downstream-most valve does not exceed 1 mile (rather than requiring valves on both sides of each crossing). This mechanism offers flexibility consistent with previous PHMSA approvals under §195.260.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shut-off segment scope for new/replaced HCA or Class 3/4 segments
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'shut-off segment' must contain the newly constructed or replaced HCA or Class 3 or Class 4 pipeline segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA clarifies its intent in §§192.634 and 195.418: where a new or entirely replaced pipeline segment is in (or, for hazardous liquid lines, could affect) an HCA, the entirety of that new/replaced segment is included in the shut-off segment for RMV/alternative-equivalent-technology requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Opportunistic’ approach for replacement projects in non-HCA Class 1 and Class 2 locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacement projects in non-HCA Class 1 and Class 2 locations do not require RMVs or alternative equivalent technology unless the replacement project involves the addition, replacement, or removal of a valve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects industry 'opportunistic approach' recommended by Committees and LPAC. The requirement does not apply to Class 1 or Class 2 locations with a PIR of 150 feet or less. For hazardous liquid pipelines, the same approach applies to replacements in non-HCA locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for RMV/alternative at pipeline termination (and acceptable equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: An RMV or alternative equivalent technology is needed at the termination of a pipeline; a manual compressor station valve at a continuously manned station may be used as an alternative equivalent technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA recognizes logical terminations within stations and allows a continuously manned compressor station valve to serve as equivalent without advance notification under §§192.18 or 195.18. However, as with other alternatives, it must be able to be closed as soon as practicable and absolutely within 30 minutes after rupture identification and comply with applicable rule provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational block valves within shut-off segments and proximity of RMVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational block valves are allowed within a shut-off segment between compliant RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies; RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies need not be the nearest valve to a shut-off segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA removed the NPRM phrase requiring 'all valves in a shut-off segment' to be RMVs/alternatives, preserving operator flexibility to install additional block valves between appropriately spaced compliant RMVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve status monitoring — pressures/flows as primary detection signals
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA expects all valves installed as RMVs and as alternative equivalent technologies to monitor pressures upstream and downstream of those valves at all times to identify ruptures effectively and mitigate incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring of upstream/downstream pressures (or flows) is considered important to identify and locate ruptures. Where real-time monitoring of pressures or flows at an ASV or a manual shut-off valve enables identification and location of a rupture, operators do not need to continuously monitor valve status or station personnel at manual valve sites. PHMSA specifies that operators need not monitor pressures on manual valves used as alternative equivalent technology once those valves are closed in response to a rupture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance to monitor pressures/flows in lieu of continuous valve status monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: If operators can remotely monitor either pressures or flows in real-time at an ASV or a manual shut-off valve such that they can identify and locate a rupture, the operator does not need to monitor valve status continually, nor are operators required to monitor pressures on manual valves being used as alternative equivalent technology once those valves are closed in response to a rupture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stems from Committee recommendations; it relieves operators from continuous valve-status monitoring if pressure/flow monitoring provides adequate rupture detection and location. It also permits not stationing personnel at a manually operated alternative-equivalent site if real-time monitoring is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-to-point verification testing for automated/remote-control valves retained
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA retains proposed point-to-point testing requirements for RMVs that are ASVs or RCVs, despite duplication with control room management regulations (§§192.631 and 195.446).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA states restating the point-to-point provision improves clarity and enforceability. Commenters asked to remove it as duplicative, but PHMSA kept it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of RMV/installation and spacing requirements to class location changes
rubrics_metrics.description: RMV and alternative equivalent technology installation and valve spacing requirements apply to class location-based pipeline replacements of 2 or more miles within any 5 contiguous miles; PHMSA expects compliance within 24 months of the class location change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA intended the requirements to apply where operators choose to replace pipe to meet MAOP requirements after a class location change. PHMSA allows operators to comply by installing or using existing RMVs so that the distance between RMVs does not exceed 20 miles in certain class-change contexts (e.g., allowing automation instead of installing new manual valves). This considers industry concerns about cost and practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for very short pipe replacements and automation option for intermediate lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception: short pipeline replacements that are less than 1,000 feet in length within 1 contiguous mile are exempt from RMV and alternative equivalent technology installation requirements. For replacements between 1,000 feet and 2 miles in length, operators may automate existing valves with RCV or ASV technologies and corresponding pressure sensors consistent with operational and spacing requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions respond to industry concerns that requiring new valves for very short replacements is impractical and costly. For 1,000 ft–2 mile replacements, automation of existing valves (with sensors) is allowed to meet objectives without installing new manual valves, consistent with GPAC recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve maintenance, inspections, and drill requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must perform inspections, maintenance, and drills on RMVs to ensure they can be closed as soon as practicable (and meet the rule's maximum valve-closure time). Proposals included point-to-point verification tests for ASVs/RCVs and initial validation and periodic confirmation drills for manual or locally operated valves identified as RMVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA clarifies annual drills apply only to manually operated valves used as alternative equivalent technology, not to ASVs or RCVs. Annual drills are required for one randomly selected manual valve in each operator's field work units; the random selection method must be in written procedures for inspection. Full closure is not required for drills; at minimum a 25 percent valve closure demonstrates operability. PHMSA does not permit tabletop drills to satisfy response-time verification because they cannot confirm real travel/operation times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelines and procedures after a failed drill (temporary measures and repair deadlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a failed drill, operators must designate a temporary alternate compliant valve within 7 days and repair or remediate the inoperable valve within 12 months. PHMSA provides an advance notification process for operators to request (before repair) an extension of the 12-month repair period by demonstrating infeasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA originally proposed shorter timeframes but extended repair period to 12 months in final rule while retaining the 7-day identification requirement. PHMSA declines to permit notification to extend the 7-day deadline for identifying alternate shut-off measures. Alternative compliant valves identified after a failed drill are not required to comply with spacing requirements but must contain the entire shut-off segment and comply with the rule's 30-minute valve-closure standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective actions, lessons learned, and training expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must identify corrective actions and lessons learned from validation and confirmation drills and share and implement those lessons throughout their pipeline systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters requested more explicit training and maintenance program requirements; PHMSA notes that operator qualification and control room management regulations already address specialized equipment and personnel training, but PHMSA expects drill results to inform procedures and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve performance standard — maximum closure time
rubrics_metrics.description: Valves (RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies) must be able to be closed as soon as is practicable and absolutely within 30 minutes after the rupture identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 30-minute absolute closure standard is reiterated throughout the final rule's installation, maintenance, and alternative-equivalent provisions. Some NPRM text proposed 40 minutes; the final rule uses the 30-minute closure standard for RMVs/alternatives and for alternative compliant valves identified after failed drills.
